clue.text: Stay for day in 23D town

parts.note: to bide is to stay or wait
taken as written
D is the standard abbreviation for day

explanation.surface: A holiday maker stopping over for a day in a Devon town.
explanation.walkthrough: 23D is DEVON, so the definition points to a Devon town; BIDEFORD is a port on the north Devon coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Bideford is a small market and port town located in north Devon, England.

clue.text: Drool over most of classiest clothing (topless)

indicators.note: most of something is all but a small part, so the final letter goes
without a top means the first letter, the top of a down light, is removed

parts.note: classiest is BEST, cut short by its last letter
clobber is British slang for clothes or gear; its first letter goes

explanation.surface: Someone salivating over an expensive, rather revealing outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: Clobber is British slang for clothing, so 'clothing (topless)' is CLOBBER without its C.
explanation.definitionFit: To beslobber is to slobber all over something, or to fawn on it excessively; both senses fit drooling.

clue.text: Only daughter turning up in Greek island

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning upward makes the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: sole means only, as in sole heir
D is the standard abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: An only child arriving on a Greek island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Only daughter' looks like one idea, but it is two pieces, SOLE and D, which are then flipped.
explanation.definitionFit: Delos is a small island in the Cyclades, celebrated in myth as the birthplace of Apollo and Artemis.

clue.text: Dazzling, not entirely dull and retiring

indicators.note: not the entire word means it loses a letter, here its last

parts.note: dull is FLAT, missing its final letter
a retiring person is shy and reserved

explanation.surface: A paradoxical description of someone both brilliant and dull and bashful.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface contradicts itself on purpose: the dull and retiring parts build the word that means the opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: Something flashy is showy and ostentatious, attracting attention the way a dazzling display does.

clue.text: Move to agitate about what?

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one piece goes round another

parts.note: to rouse is to stir up or agitate
eh? is a request to repeat, like 'what?'

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about why anyone would bother stirring things up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'what?' is not a question to the solver but the interjection EH, which sits inside the stirring word.
explanation.definitionFit: To rehouse people is to move them to new accommodation, so the verb fits 'Move' as a transitive verb.

clue.text: Page tucking into mouldy bread, perhaps

indicators.note: someone tucking into food gets inside it, so one piece enters another

parts.note: mouldy food is old and stale
P is the standard abbreviation for page

explanation.surface: A page boy eating some mouldy bread.
explanation.walkthrough: Page looks like a servant boy eating, but it is just the letter P. 'perhaps' marks bread as one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A staple is a basic everyday food, and bread is a classic example of such a basic foodstuff.

clue.text: A lot of rubbish about a French jibe

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one piece goes round another

parts.note: tat is cheap, shoddy goods, a lot of junk
un is French for 'a'

explanation.surface: Someone dismissing a French insult as a load of nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: Tat is British for tacky junk. 'a French' means the French word for a, not a French person.
explanation.definitionFit: A taunt is a mocking or provoking remark, the same as a jibe or jeer.

clue.text: Flat pack in 17 town

parts.note: a pad is slang for one's flat or home
to stow is to pack away

explanation.surface: Self-assembly flat-pack furniture being delivered in a Cornish town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flat pack' reads as one furniture term but splits into two words. 17 is CORNWALL; Padstow is a fishing port on its north coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Padstow is a harbour town on the north coast of Cornwall, famous for seafood restaurants.

clue.text: Start of exciting times, replanting tree in 23D city

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of the word

indicators.note: to replant is to put down again in a new arrangement

parts.note: X is the multiplication sign, read as 'times'
taken as written

explanation.surface: An exciting time of tree-planting in a Devon city.
explanation.walkthrough: 23D is DEVON; Exeter is its county city. 'times' is the multiplication sign X.
explanation.definitionFit: Exeter is a cathedral city and the county town of Devon in south-west England.

clue.text: Sailor remains in 17 town

parts.note: an old salt is an experienced sailor
ash is what remains after burning

explanation.surface: A sailor staying on in a Cornish town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'remains' looks like a verb, as if the sailor stays, but it is the noun: what is left after a fire. 17 is CORNWALL.
explanation.definitionFit: Saltash is a Cornish town on the River Tamar, across the water from Plymouth in Devon.

clue.text: Possibly loud frolics after receiving honour? On the contrary

indicators.note: to receive something is to take it in, so one piece holds another
this reverses the roles stated, so the holder and the held swap places

parts.note: CBE, Commander of the Order of the British Empire, is a British honour

indicators.note: frolicking letters leap around playfully into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Noisy high jinks breaking out after someone receives a royal honour.
explanation.walkthrough: As written, the shuffled word would hold the honour; 'On the contrary' flips it so the CBE holds the shuffled letters. 'after' is only padding linking the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something could be means it is possible, so the phrase works as an adverbial 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Chlorine this writer found in encyclopaedia as 'something mild'

definitions.note: the answer is a noun for mildness, so this is a loose 'something mild'

parts.note: Cl is the chemical symbol for chlorine

indicators.note: what is found in something lies inside it, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: ENCY is a dictionary abbreviation for encyclopaedia
the setter refers to themself as this writer

explanation.surface: A writer looking up chlorine in an encyclopaedia and finding it described as mild.
explanation.walkthrough: 'this writer' is the setter, giving ME, which goes inside the abbreviation ENCY; chlorine's symbol stands in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Clemency means mildness, whether merciful leniency in judgement or gentle temperate weather.

clue.text: You once slipped into a vessel in Old English kiln's environment

indicators.note: slipping into something means getting inside it
being in something means being enclosed by it

parts.note: OE is the standard abbreviation for Old English
taken as written
SS, steamship, is a vessel
thou is the old form of 'you'

explanation.surface: An archaic tale of someone slipping onto an old English boat.
explanation.walkthrough: There are two layers of containment, with 'in' wrapping the first result inside the second. An oast house is a building in Kent where hops are dried.
explanation.definitionFit: An oast house is the building housing a kiln for drying hops, so it surrounds the kiln.

clue.text: Fedora? Trilby? (Hat encompassing latest in comfort)

indicators.note: to encompass is to surround, so one piece goes round another

parts.note: tile is old slang for a hat

indicators.note: the latest letter of a word is its last one

parts.note: last letter of the word

explanation.surface: Wondering which comfortable hat to pick: a fedora or a trilby.
explanation.walkthrough: Fedora and Trilby look like hats but are titles: Fedora is a play by Sardou, Trilby a novel by George du Maurier, each named after its heroine.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are names of literary works, a play and a novel, so each is an example of a title.

clue.text: European seen with mate in 17 town

parts.note: bud is short for buddy, a mate
E is the standard abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A European tourist spotted with a friend in a Cornish town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seen with' only puts the pieces side by side, in either order; here the mate comes first. 17 is CORNWALL.
explanation.definitionFit: Bude is a seaside resort town on the north-east coast of Cornwall, popular for surfing.

clue.text: Turmoil about theatre, concerts etc? Refuse to go in them

parts.note: dust, as in a dust-up, is a commotion or row
c, circa, means about
theatre and concerts are among the arts

explanation.surface: A culture boycott: chaos over the arts and a refusal to attend any events.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' reads as a verb, declining to attend, but it is the noun: rubbish. A dustcart is the British name for a garbage truck.
explanation.definitionFit: Dustcarts are council trucks that collect household rubbish, so refuse goes into them.

clue.text: Herbal medicine's fine, always given to a small number

parts.note: F is the pencil grading for fine
ever means always, as in ever hopeful
a few is a small number

explanation.surface: A herbal remedy is good and should always be taken by a few people.
explanation.walkthrough: The ’s stands for 'is', joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Feverfew is a daisy-like plant whose leaves are traditionally taken as a herbal remedy for migraines.

clue.text: Electric device enthusiast beginning to harass consumer

parts.note: a fan is an enthusiast

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of the word
an eater consumes food

explanation.surface: A gadget fan starting to pester shoppers about an electrical product.
explanation.walkthrough: 'consumer' suggests a shopper, but here it is someone who consumes food.
explanation.definitionFit: A fan heater is an electrical appliance that blows air across a heating element to warm a room.

clue.text: Hackneyed comments on side of building in neighbour of 23D

indicators.note: in a down entry, one piece sitting on another comes above it

parts.note: corn is trite, sentimental material
a wall forms the side of a building

explanation.surface: Tired graffiti on the side of a building in Devon's neighbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 23D is DEVON, which borders the answer to the east.
explanation.definitionFit: Cornwall is the county directly west of Devon, sharing the River Tamar as their border.

clue.text: Special information reveals stagnation

parts.note: S is an abbreviation for special
the lowdown is the inside information

explanation.surface: A news headline: leaked data exposes economic stagnation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Special information' reads as one phrase, like special intelligence, but splits into S and the informal word for the facts.
explanation.definitionFit: A slowdown is a reduction in activity or growth, close to economic stagnation.

clue.text: Recover and relax increasingly, but not at first

indicators.note: without its first, a word loses its opening letter

parts.note: to rest is to relax
increasingly is MORE and MORE; the word MORE loses its first letter

explanation.surface: Advice for convalescence: get better and take it easier, though not right away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'increasingly' is here the word MORE, as in 'more and more'.
explanation.definitionFit: To restore something is to bring it back to its former condition, as when one recovers lost ground.

clue.text: Isolated figure receiving instructions in middle of week

indicators.note: to receive something is to take it in, so one piece holds another
the middle of a four-letter word is its two central letters

parts.note: the middle two letters of the word
a remit is a set of instructions or terms of reference

explanation.surface: A lonely figure receiving orders midweek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'figure' tempts towards a number, but the definition is the whole phrase for a recluse.
explanation.definitionFit: An eremite is a hermit, especially a Christian recluse living alone in the desert.

clue.text: Authority against 50% of malicious web behaviour

indicators.note: fifty per cent is half, so half the letters are lost

parts.note: con means against, as in pros and cons
trolling is posting malicious provocation online; its first half is kept

explanation.surface: Authorities pushing back against the worst of online abuse.
explanation.walkthrough: The behaviour is TROLLING, eight letters, so half of it is the first four.
explanation.definitionFit: Control means power or command over something, which is what authority is.

clue.text: Showing warmth and pity in 17 town

parts.note: red is the colour of warmth and heat
ruth is an old word for pity, as in ruthless

explanation.surface: Kindness and compassion shown in a Cornish town.
explanation.walkthrough: RUTH survives in modern English mainly through 'ruthless', without pity. 17 is CORNWALL.
explanation.definitionFit: Redruth is a former tin-mining town in west Cornwall, next to Camborne.

clue.text: Put off carrying tin, having bottle

indicators.note: carrying something means holding it inside

parts.note: to deter is to put off
a can is a tin

explanation.surface: Someone discouraged from drinking out of a tin, having found a bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put off' looks like a verb about delaying, but it means discourage.
explanation.definitionFit: A decanter is a glass bottle, usually stoppered, into which wine or spirits are poured for serving.

clue.text: Study covering very old neighbour of 17

indicators.note: a covering goes round what it covers

parts.note: a den is a study or private room
V is the standard abbreviation for very
O is the standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: Research into an ancient neighbour of Cornwall.
explanation.walkthrough: 17 is CORNWALL, its western neighbour.
explanation.definitionFit: Devon is the English county immediately east of Cornwall, the two sharing a border along the Tamar.

clue.text: Each day coming in to cut field

indicators.note: pieces coming in go inside another

parts.note: to mow is to cut grass
EA is the standard abbreviation for each
D is the standard abbreviation for day

explanation.surface: A farmhand turning up daily to cut a field.
explanation.walkthrough: The mowing word opens to take in the two abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: A meadow is a grassy field, often one where hay is grown and cut.

clue.text: Guided to secure new grant

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it firmly inside

parts.note: led is the past tense of lead, to guide
N is the standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: Someone steered towards obtaining fresh funding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grant' looks like a noun, a sum of money, but the answer is the verb, as in lend support.
explanation.definitionFit: To lend can mean to give or impart, as in lend weight or lend assistance, matching grant.

clue.text: Flexible Minister backed steps to seal off area

indicators.note: going backwards makes the letters read right to left

parts.note: Rev, Reverend, is a title for a minister of religion

indicators.note: sealing something off encloses it completely

parts.note: a stile is a set of steps over a fence or wall
A is the standard abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: An adaptable minister retreating and taking steps to cordon off a zone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minister' suggests a government figure, but here it is a clergyman, abbreviated Rev.
explanation.definitionFit: Versatile means adaptable to many uses or tasks, so it is a synonym of flexible.

clue.text: Real dispute tails off in city in 17

indicators.note: with tails off, each word loses its last letter

parts.note: real is TRUE, minus its final letter
a dispute is a ROW, minus its final letter

explanation.surface: A genuine quarrel fizzling out in a Cornish city.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words lose their tails, plural. 17 is CORNWALL, whose only city this is.
explanation.definitionFit: Truro is the only city in Cornwall, with a cathedral and the county's administrative centre.

clue.text: Contributing to klaxon, as a lover of hooters

indicators.note: something contributing to a phrase supplies part of it, so the letters lie inside the words

parts.note: runs across the end of the first word through the start of the last

explanation.surface: Someone who loves car horns adding to the din.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hooters' looks like car horns, matching the klaxon, but hooter is British slang for a nose.
explanation.definitionFit: Nasal means relating to the nose, and hooter is a slang name for the nose.

clue.text: Target or point in receiving injection of hard brain chemical

indicators.note: an injection puts something inside, so one piece goes into another

parts.note: an end is an aim or target
taken as written
a pin has a sharp point
H is the pencil grading for hard

explanation.surface: A needle point receiving a dose of a hard drug.
explanation.walkthrough: The injection image is apt: the H goes into the PIN, as a needle goes into skin.
explanation.definitionFit: Endorphins are neurotransmitters released by the brain and pituitary gland that relieve pain and lift mood.
